summary: Point Fermin Light, San Pedro, Los Angeles: a wooden tower first lit 15 December 1874 by two sisters, dark since 1941, saved in the 1970s and now owned by the city.

light.characteristic: flashing white (changed from fixed white in 1889 to flashing in 1912; the record's Fl W 10s describes the later pole light)

lens.where: ground floor of the lighthouse, after recovery in 2006 from a Malibu real estate office

structures.note: Integral light tower and residence. The record gives 9.0 m; the Los Angeles Times describes a 55-foot tower. Lantern, railings and lens removed in 1942, and a woodshed-type shelter placed on the tower (NRHP); a new lantern room was built in the 1970s.
Wartime lookout shelter on the tower, known locally as the chicken coop (LighthouseFriends; NRHP).
Beacon on a plain pole near the bluff, mounted after the war (LA Times); the NRHP nomination describes a separate audio beacon elsewhere on the point.

access.note: The point is a city park, Point Fermin Park. LighthouseFriends says the lighthouse has opened to visitors; a 2002 Times article said the grounds were open and the interior was not.

facts.agency: City of Los Angeles (awarded 2015, transfer December 2018, per LighthouseFriends); the 2002 Times article called the light Coast Guard-owned

events.note: Congress appropriates $20,000 for a lighthouse and fog signal in June
Court rules for the government on condemnation, 4 November 1873
Wooden tower and residence built with redwood and fir delivered by ship; work begins 21 February 1874
Lit 15 December 1874 by Mary L. Smith and her sister Ella
Mary L. Smith, head keeper, first keeper
George N. Shaw, head keeper, to 1904
Flashing red and white changed to fixed white, 1 April 1889
Changed to flashing (Lighthouse Service Bulletin lists Point Fermin among lights changed from fixed to flashing or occulting)
Commissioner's report proposes a new light at Point Vicente and says Point Fermin would then be discontinued
Willie L. Austin, head keeper, with his family
German U-boat towed out and sunk off Point Fermin by Coast Guard and destroyer (LA Times)
Oil lamps replaced by a powerful electric light reaching 18 miles (NRHP); the Times dates the final changeover later
Thelma Austin, head keeper, to 1927
Steamer David C. Meyer aground; no lives lost (LA Times); the NRHP nomination lists the David C. Meyer among ships lost
Thelma Austin's service ends; Los Angeles Park Department agreement with the Lighthouse Service (LighthouseFriends)
Long Beach earthquake, 10 March 1933: Point Fermin's old combined dwelling and tower reported not damaged
Extinguished 9 December 1941, two days after Pearl Harbor (LighthouseFriends); the Times says within hours of the attack
Coast Guard turns the light off for security; tower painted; radar lookout use (NRHP); experimental Navy radar station (LA Times)
Lantern room removed; lookout shelter placed on the tower (LighthouseFriends; NRHP gives 1942 for removal of lantern, railings and lens; the form's date is partly unclear in OCR)
Los Angeles regains possession and makes the lighthouse a residence for a park maintenance supervisor
Added to the National Register of Historic Places, June 1972 (LighthouseFriends; NRHP form dated 1971)
Restoration with new lantern room and gallery; centennial celebration 2 November 1974
Fresnel lens recovered from a Malibu real estate office on 13 November 2006 and returned to display in the lighthouse
Lighthouse awarded to the City of Los Angeles, 20 January 2015
Formal transfer of the lighthouse, December 2018

keepers.name: Mary L. Smith
keepers.note: First keeper; with her sister Ella came from Ediz Hook, Washington (LighthouseFriends; USLHS). The Los Angeles Times names the sister Helen; USLHS and LighthouseFriends give Ella.

keepers.name: Ella T. Smith
keepers.note: Sister of Mary L. Smith; USLHS records her at Ediz Hook as first assistant 1871-1873 before Point Fermin

keepers.name: George N. Shaw
keepers.note: Held the post more than two decades, living at the lighthouse with his wife and daughter (LA Times). The Shaws watched the Respigadera in 1888.

keepers.name: Willie L. Austin
keepers.note: Also written William L. Austin (LA Times); moved in 1917 with his wife and children (LighthouseFriends; LA Times). Died 1925, about three months after his wife, according to the Times; LighthouseFriends gives two months.

keepers.name: Martha M. Austin
keepers.note: Roster reads 1917 to at least 1921. The LA Times describes Martha Bunce Austin as his wife and helper, paid $300 a year.

keepers.name: Thelma Austin
keepers.note: Daughter of Willie and Martha Austin, aged 24 when she applied; kept the light until 1927 (LighthouseFriends; LA Times)

wrecks.outcome: British vessel; NRHP says it struck a rock and sank within 20 minutes; LA Times says it was forced into deeper water and destroyed by dynamite. The sources disagree.
Aground, no lives lost (LA Times); listed among ships lost by the NRHP nomination
Lumber schooner, listed among ships lost off the point (NRHP)
Towed out to sea and sunk by a destroyer's shells off Point Fermin, watched by the Austin family (LA Times)

notes_for_editor: Newspaper search (Chronicling America via newspapers.py) for Point Fermin was attempted and failed with HTTP 520 from loc.gov; the 1874-1883 and 1888 newspaper checks were not made. Sources 1 and 3 are copyrighted: facts restated in our words, with at most one short phrase quoted from each in the published story. The LA Park page (recreation.parks.lacity.gov) refused both fetch_text and WebFetch with HTTP 403. The USCG Historian's page refused archive copies. Conflicts to a human reviewer: (a) the second sister is Ella (LighthouseFriends, USLHS) or Helen (LA Times); the USLHS record also calls Ella a sister of a keeper Cynthia Smith and a daughter of keeper George K. Smith, which no other source checked here mentions; (b) the Respigadera's fate is a sinking (NRHP) or a dynamited wreck after a grounding (LA Times); (c) the David C. Meyer 1926 event is an aground with no lives lost (LA Times) and a ship lost (NRHP); (d) electrification is 1925 (NRHP) or later, with Thelma's job ending (LA Times), while LighthouseFriends says she kept the light until 1927; (e) deactivation is 9 December 1941 (LighthouseFriends) or 'within hours' of Pearl Harbor (LA Times); the NRHP text reads 'until 1942', which is probably an OCR of 1941; (f) the removal of the lantern is dated 1941-1942; (g) Willie Austin's wife died two months before him (LighthouseFriends) or three months (LA Times); (h) the 1874 tower height is 9.0 m (record) or 55 ft (LA Times); the record's focal height 36.6 m and characteristic belong to the later pole light. The NRHP nomination's OCR is poor for dates. The 'wartime green' phrase and the radar-lookout wording are read cleanly and are quoted. The story does not rely on the NRHP's 'until 19^2' reading, which the 1941 date from LighthouseFriends and the Times makes almost certainly 1941; the page image was not checked for it. The 'December 15' reading agrees with LighthouseFriends and the Times. The story now states the Times' three-months and LighthouseFriends' two-months accounts of Willie Austin's death and the Times' 'three years later' electrification date beside the NRHP's 1925 date. Roster role headings are normalised: 'Principal Lighthouse Keeper' is head keeper, 'Laborer' is laborer. Several keepers and family members here are named from the sources only; no private residents of the present-day lighthouse are named.
